title: CI: consider adding npm dependency caching to setup-node step
need_summary: The developer asked if npm dependency caching can be added to the CI workflow and whether it poses a security risk; the maintainer answered that caching must be disabled without a lockfile per the actions/setup-node documentation (see the advanced‑usage docs) and noted potential cache‑pollution attacks.
security_topic: caching disabled due to missing lockfile and potential CI cache pollution
question_text:
I was exploring the CI workflow as part of my university project on GitHub Actions and noticed that the setup-node step doesn't currently include dependency caching.

The current setup-node step looks like this:

- uses: actions/setup-node@6044e13b5dc448c55e2357c09f80417699197238 # v6.2.0
  with:
    node-version: 'lts/*'

Adding cache: 'npm' would allow GitHub Actions to cache node_modules between runs, which can reduce install time on repeated builds:

- uses: actions/setup-node@6044e13b5dc448c55e2357c09f80417699197238 # v6.2.0
  with:
    node-version: 'lts/*'
    cache: 'npm'

I tested this on my own Node.js project and it worked without any other changes needed. I appreciate this may already be a considered decision, so happy to hear if there's a reason it's been left out.
answer_text:
I guess I found out why we don't use cache for CI. Express does not have a `package-lock.json`[^1] (https://github.com/expressjs/express/issues/4619, https://github.com/expressjs/express/issues/3963#issuecomment-493460138) and the `actions/setup-node` [documentation](https://github.com/actions/setup-node/blob/670825a89dc0abd596e7a3abd0f5e3f6e5faf37c/docs/advanced-usage.md#running-without-a-lockfile) says:

> If you choose not to use a lockfile, you must ensure that **caching is disabled**. The `cache` feature relies on the lockfile to generate a unique key for the cache entry.
thread_text:
ISSUE #7196: CI: consider adding npm dependency caching to setup-node step
Author: eddieteall
Date: 2026-04-21T20:00:16Z
Labels: question
State: closed

[c0]
I was exploring the CI workflow as part of my university project on GitHub Actions and noticed that the setup-node step doesn't currently include dependency caching.

The current setup-node step looks like this:

- uses: actions/setup-node@6044e13b5dc448c55e2357c09f80417699197238 # v6.2.0
  with:
    node-version: 'lts/*'

Adding cache: 'npm' would allow GitHub Actions to cache node_modules between runs, which can reduce install time on repeated builds:

- uses: actions/setup-node@6044e13b5dc448c55e2357c09f80417699197238 # v6.2.0
  with:
    node-version: 'lts/*'
    cache: 'npm'

I tested this on my own Node.js project and it worked without any other changes needed. I appreciate this may already be a considered decision, so happy to hear if there's a reason it's been left out.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @krzysdz 2026-04-21T21:18:03Z:
I looked at the history and caching is not mentioned anywhere in #5599, which reworked the CI. The older Appveyor CI did [cache `node_modules`](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/c96c690dc087d121137c97318215e03a432395c5/appveyor.yml#L22-L23), so maybe everyone just missed this.

The "Install dependencies" step does not take a lot of time (7-15 seconds on ubuntu runners; 20+ on windows), but I think it's enough for cache to make it faster. GitHub only stores cache for [7 days](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching#usage-limits-and-eviction-policy:~:text=GitHub%20will%20remove%20any%20cache%20entries%20that%20have%20not%20been%20accessed%20in%20over%207%20days%2E) and there have been periods when CI did not run for more than this[^1]. Saving cache will make the execution time a bit longer, but in my opinion it is not something that we should care about.

Finally, cache can allow compromising CI though cache pollution (evict cache and then make GitHub save your version with malicious additions, which will then be used to install dependencies). This is also not a problem for us, because running actions requires maintainer approval (though I'm not completely sure about this) and workflows that could use cache ([ci](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/8e022edc9185f540a3fcecaf5e56b850d919cdac/.github/workflows/ci.yml#L16-L17) and [legacy](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/8e022edc9185f540a3fcecaf5e56b850d919cdac/.github/workflows/legacy.yml#L18-L19)) have read-only [`contents` permissions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#permissions).

[^1]: Adding [scheduled runs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) would allow avoiding cache expiry and, more importantly, help us faster detect regressions caused by dependency updates.
---
[c2] @krzysdz 2026-05-06T22:56:01Z:
I guess I found out why we don't use cache for CI. Express does not have a `package-lock.json`[^1] (https://github.com/expressjs/express/issues/4619, https://github.com/expressjs/express/issues/3963#issuecomment-493460138) and the `actions/setup-node` [documentation](https://github.com/actions/setup-node/blob/670825a89dc0abd596e7a3abd0f5e3f6e5faf37c/docs/advanced-usage.md#running-without-a-lockfile) says:

> If you choose not to use a lockfile, you must ensure that **caching is disabled**. The `cache` feature relies on the lockfile to generate a unique key for the cache entry.

[^1]: enforced by [`.npmrc`](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/f873ac23124ffcff8c040b4bd257b32c29828d53/.npmrc) and [`.gitignore`](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/f873ac23124ffcff8c040b4bd257b32c29828d53/.gitignore#L3)

title: Vulnerable dependency version that is 12 years old: path-to-regexp
need_summary: The developer needed to know if the reported vulnerable path-to-regexp version is actually vulnerable and which safe version to use; the answer points to the Snyk advisory showing version 0.1.13 is not vulnerable and advises updating to 0.1.13 (see Snyk URL and Express package.json).
security_topic: dependency version vulnerability and update guidance
question_text: Vulnerable dependency version that is 12 years old: path-to-regexp
answer_text:
I'm not sure what you mean. Express 4 uses `path-to-regexp` versions `0.1.x` and Express 4.22.1 specifies `path-to-regexp` version as [`~0.1.12`](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/v4.22.1/package.json#L54) (#7135), which should install [0.1.13](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v.0.1.13) that was released 5 days ago.

The Snyk page shows that [0.1.13](https://security.snyk.io/package/npm/path-to-regexp/0.1.13) is not known to be affected by any vulnerabilities. The description on that page says _Published: 13 years ago_, but also _Last updated: 10 hours ago_.

If you have an older version installed, please run `npm update path-to-regexp` or `npm audit fix`. Fresh installs (without `node_modules`) should also install `path-to-regexp@0.1.13` on `npm install`. The official [blog post](https://expressjs.com/2026/03/30/security-releases.html) also suggests running `npm update path-to-regexp`.

title: View.prototype.lookup() lacks path containment check (unlike send library for res.sendFile)
need_summary: The developer asked if the path‑traversal issue in View.prototype.lookup() can be fixed, and the maintainer pointed to PR #7142 as the concrete fix.
security_topic: path traversal risk in view rendering via res.render
question_text: `View.prototype.lookup()` in `lib/view.js:104-123` uses `path.resolve(root, name)` without validating that the resolved path stays within the configured views directory. Combined with `decodeURIComponent()` in route parameter decoding, applications that pass user input to `res.render()` are exposed to path traversal.
answer_text:
Thanks for the detailed report.

After reviewing `lib/view.js`, the `res.render()` docs, and prior discussion in #4445, this looks like **working as designed** rather than a new security bug.

- `View.prototype.lookup()` resolves from the configured `views` path but does not enforce containment, and `res.render()` intentionally supports absolute view paths.
- This behavior is covered by tests (`test/res.render.js` and `test/app.render.js` include absolute path rendering).
- The API docs already warn that the `view` argument should not contain end-user input because it performs filesystem operations.

`res.sendFile()` is different by design: it uses `send`, which applies traversal protections (especially when `root` is set) because that API is commonly used with user-influenced file paths.

I’d triage this as a **security hardening enhancement** (defense in depth), not a vulnerability/regression. A default containment change would likely be breaking, so 6.x (or an opt-in strict mode in 5.x) plus docs updates seems like the safest path.
thread_text:
ISSUE #7140: View.prototype.lookup() lacks path containment check (unlike send library for res.sendFile)
Author: raajheshkannaa
Date: 2026-03-30T22:24:19Z
Labels: enhancement, security, require-triage
State: open

[c0]
## Description

`View.prototype.lookup()` in `lib/view.js:104-123` uses `path.resolve(root, name)` without validating that the resolved path stays within the configured views directory. Combined with `decodeURIComponent()` in route parameter decoding, applications that pass user input to `res.render()` are exposed to path traversal.

`res.sendFile()` has path traversal protection via the `send` library's root containment check. The view system has no equivalent protection.

## Reproduction

```javascript
const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.set('views', __dirname + '/views');
app.set('view engine', 'ejs');
app.get('/page/:name', (req, res) => res.render(req.params.name));
app.listen(3000);
```

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/page/..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd
```

Route param decodes to `../../../../etc/passwd`. View lookup resolves outside views directory.

Runtime verification on Express 5.2.1:
```javascript
layer.match('/page/..%2f..%2fetc%2fpasswd')
// => true, params.name = "../../etc/passwd"
```

## Context

This is not a critical vulnerability since it requires the developer to pass unsanitized user input to `res.render()`. However, given that `res.sendFile()` already has containment via the `send` library, adding equivalent protection in `View.prototype.lookup()` would provide defense-in-depth consistency.

## Suggested improvement

```javascript
// lib/view.js - View.prototype.lookup()
var loc = resolve(root, name);
if (!loc.startsWith(resolve(root) + sep)) continue;
```

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @som14062005 2026-03-31T08:15:00Z:
I've submitted a fix for this in PR #7142. Happy to make any changes
if the approach needs adjustment.
---
[c2] @krzysdz 2026-03-31T17:07:28Z:
This is a known behaviour (#4445), but I agree that changing this is a good idea. I can't think of a reason why anyone would try to render something outside of the views directory, but that doesn't mean that nobody does this.

This probably requires a major release (6.x?) and documentation changes.
---
[c3] @som14062005 2026-03-31T17:22:44Z:
Thanks for the context on #4445 i understand this could be a 
breaking change for users rendering files outside the views directory.

happy to:
- Retarget this to 6.x if that's preferred
- Add an opt-in setting for 5.x instead
- Include documentation changes

Please let me know how you'd like to proceed.
---
[c4] @IamLizu 2026-04-04T18:50:37Z:
Thanks for the detailed report.

After reviewing `lib/view.js`, the `res.render()` docs, and prior discussion in #4445, this looks like **working as designed** rather than a new security bug.

- `View.prototype.lookup()` resolves from the configured `views` path but does not enforce containment, and `res.render()` intentionally supports absolute view paths.
- This behavior is covered by tests (`test/res.render.js` and `test/app.render.js` include absolute path rendering).
- The API docs already warn that the `view` argument should not contain end-user input because it performs filesystem operations.

`res.sendFile()` is different by design: it uses `send`, which applies traversal protections (especially when `root` is set) because that API is commonly used with user-influenced file paths.

I’d triage this as a **security hardening enhancement** (defense in depth), not a vulnerability/regression. A default containment change would likely be breaking, so 6.x (or an opt-in strict mode in 5.x) plus docs updates seems like the safest path.

title: update to `qs@^6.14.1`
need_summary: The developer needed to know if the qs vulnerability (CVE-2025-15284 / GHSA-6rw7-vpxm-498p) is fixed in Express, and the answer cites specific Express versions (e.g., 4.22.1 and 5.2.1) with package.json links showing they depend on qs ≥ 6.14.1, confirming the fix.
security_topic: express dependency includes patched qs version for CVE-2025-15284
question_text: A few days ago, the following security flaw was discovered in lib qs. However, no issue or PR was found regarding this flaw or a possible solution. Projects that use Express are vulnerable and without solutions for the flaw. Please let us know when you can. Thank you!
answer_text:
In this case, the reported vulnerability in `qs` (CVE-2025-15284) is already addressed by default in Express. Current Express releases depend on patched versions of `qs`:

- **Express 4** specifies `"qs": "~6.14.0"`, which resolves to `>=6.14.0 <6.15.0` and therefore pulls in the patched `6.14.1` release by default. Reference: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/f62378e1bc776259c0a471476c2dc043a02ac762/package.json#L56

- **Express 5** specifies `"qs": "^6.14.0"`, which also pulls in the patched versions automatically. Reference: https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/c2fb76e99f7379b706a5510b4b2dd08a1b710b7b/package.json#L55

As a result, users installing Express without overriding dependency resolutions already receive a version of `qs` that includes the fix, and the reported issue does not represent an unpatched vulnerability in Express itself.

title: res.redirect(undefined) sends invalid Location: undefined header
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether calling res.redirect(undefined) would produce a malformed Location header and how it is addressed; the answer references PR #7103 which updates res.redirect() to throw a TypeError for missing or invalid arguments.
security_topic: invalid redirect URL handling leading to malformed Location header
question_text: Calling res.redirect(undefined) currently sends a 302 response with the header Location: undefined. While there is a deprecation warning printed to the console ("Provide a url argument"), the actual HTTP response is malformed because undefined is not a valid URL.
answer_text: Submitted a fix for this in PR #7103. The res.redirect() function now throws a TypeError immediately when called with missing or invalid arguments instead of sending a malformed Location header.
thread_text:
ISSUE #6941: res.redirect(undefined) sends invalid Location: undefined header
Author: BOXER78
Date: 2025-12-03T16:47:18Z

[c0]
Calling res.redirect(undefined) currently sends a 302 response with the header Location: undefined. While there is a deprecation warning printed to the console ("Provide a url argument"), the actual HTTP response is malformed because undefined is not a valid URL.

[c1] @bjohansebas 2025-12-11T15:25:32Z:
While it’s not a valid URL, we convert any argument to a string, which is why passing `undefined` is valid and will trigger a 302.

Ref: https://github.com/expressjs/express/issues/6391

Even `Location:` is a valid Location header per the spec.

title: sendFile fails within .git folder
need_summary: The developer needed to know how to safely serve files from a .git directory without exposing repository contents, and the answer referenced Express's `dotfiles` option documentation (see Express docs and send README) as the concrete source.
security_topic: dotfiles handling in file serving
question_text: Yet when I do this, I can access /.git/HEAD without issues?
thread_text:
ISSUE #6874: sendFile fails within .git folder
Author: Sainan
Date: 2025-11-02T14:21:53Z
Labels: bug
State: closed

[c0]
<!-- The process for bug fixing is:

- We will first assess if the behavior is different from what should occur
- Confirm the bug is reproducible
- Discuss how to best fix the bug
- Work towards a fix
-->

## Environment information

**Version**: 5.1.0
<!-- 
To find the installed version of a package, you can check the `package.json` file in the root directory of your project. The version will be listed under `dependencies` or `devDependencies`, like this:

```json
"dependencies": {
  "express": "4.18.2"
}
-->

**Platform**: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.19045.0 x64
<!-- 
UNIX: output of uname -a
Windows: output of "$([Environment]::OSVersion.VersionString) $(('x86', 'x64')[[Environment]::Is64BitOperatingSystem])" in PowerShell console 
-->

**Node.js version**: v24.6.0
<!-- 
Output of node -v.
-->

**Any other relevant information**:

## What steps will reproduce the bug?
```js
const baseDir = path.join(import.meta.dirname, ".."); // Update as required by project structure
route.get("/test", (_, res) => {
    res.sendFile(path.join(baseDir, ".git/HEAD"));
});
```
Send a request to /test. It will fail with a NotFoundError being thrown.

It does seem like `express.static` works fine with a .git root, however.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @krzysdz 2025-11-02T14:33:31Z:
The [`dotfiles` option](https://expressjs.com/en/5x/api.html#res.sendFile) of `res.sendFile` defaults to `"ignore"`. The `dotfiles` checks not only the filename but also directories ([docs](https://github.com/pillarjs/send/blob/cd0c2535f31100a4224c82deb32e93e3b07b0ac1/README.md#dotfiles), [code](https://github.com/pillarjs/send/blob/cd0c2535f31100a4224c82deb32e93e3b07b0ac1/index.js#L801-L816)).

If you want `res.sendFile` to allow files and directories starting with a dot, set `dotfiles` to `"allow"`:

```js
const baseDir = path.join(import.meta.dirname, ".."); // Update as required by project structure
route.get("/test", (_, res) => {
    res.sendFile(path.join(baseDir, ".git/HEAD"), { dotfiles: "allow" });
});
```
---
[c2] @Sainan 2025-11-02T14:36:55Z:
Yet when I do this, I can access /.git/HEAD without issues?
```js
router.use("/.git", express.static(path.join(baseDir, ".git")));
```
---
[c3] @krzysdz 2025-11-02T14:50:01Z:
The root directory is not checked, because it's something the programmer sets themselves. `dotfiles` is meant to protect from accidental leaks.

With `res.sendFile` you can set the root directory too and keep `dotfiles` at `"ignore"`:

```js
const baseDir = path.join(import.meta.dirname, ".."); // Update as required by project structure
route.get("/test", (_, res) => {
    res.sendFile("HEAD", { root: path.join(baseDir, ".git") });
});
```
---
[c4] @Sainan 2025-11-02T14:52:27Z:
Hmm, I guess the usage of `path.join` was incorrect for it, but I ended up just removing this abstraction entirely in favour of `res.send(await fs.readFile(...));`.
---

title: Router cycles cause silent runtime hangs
need_summary: The developer wanted to know if Express can detect and warn about router cycles that cause hangs (a potential denial-of-service), and the maintainer referenced PR #183 in the pillarjs/router package that adds cycle detection and emits a warning.
security_topic: router cycle detection to prevent silent runtime hangs
question_text: Detecting this setup when `app.use` / `router.use` is called and emitting a warning would make the problem much easier to diagnose, while keeping behavior unchanged.
answer_text: This issue is actually in the router package (pillarjs/router) which Express depends on. I've addressed it with cycle detection that emits a warning when a router is mounted on itself: https://github.com/pillarjs/router/pull/183
thread_text:
ISSUE #6809: Router cycles cause silent runtime hangs
Author: IlyasShabi
Date: 2025-10-06T11:56:34Z
Labels: module:router
State: open

[c0]
Express allows a router to be mounted on itself (directly or indirectly). The registration succeeds, but any request that traverses the cycle hangs indefinitely causing a stack overflow. The issue is tricky to spot because nothing happens at startup.

Detecting this setup when `app.use` / `router.use` is called and emitting a warning would make the problem much easier to diagnose, while keeping behavior unchanged.

Steps to reproduce

```
const express = require('express');
const app = express();

// Simple self-loop
const loop = express.Router();
loop.use('/', loop); // mounts router onto itself

app.use('/cycle', loop);

app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send('ok'));

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on 3000'));

```

Hit `GET /cycle` the request never completes and memory usage grows until the process terminates.


The issue is easy to introduce in complex router hierarchies and incredibly hard to debug once it manifests. Emitting a warning when such a circular mount is detected would reduce the time needed to locate the offending setup, and we can consider turning this into a thrown error in the next major version (v6).


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @aprici7y 2025-10-07T20:04:32Z:
This issue is actually in the router package (pillarjs/router) which Express depends on. I've addressed it with cycle detection that emits a warning when a router is mounted on itself: https://github.com/pillarjs/router/pull/183
---

title: The Great Monkey-Patch Safari
need_summary: The developer asked which parts of the codebase monkey‑patch Node’s HTTP core, and the answer lists the affected modules (compression, express‑session, connect‑timeout, response‑time, cookie‑session, morgan, on‑headers, express) and points to the specific on‑finished patch at commit d2974f5a18f468ea56f58acb2f6d402f4b5142f0.
security_topic: cataloguing monkey-patching of Node core modules
question_text: What else?
answer_text: `on-finish` patches assign socket https://github.com/jshttp/on-finished/blob/d2974f5a18f468ea56f58acb2f6d402f4b5142f0/index.js#L189-L199
thread_text:
ISSUE #6669: The Great Monkey-Patch Safari
Author: jonchurch
Date: 2025-07-30T21:14:26Z
Labels: discuss
State: open

[c0]
We want to track down and document all instances of express and our core deps monkey-patching Node core, specifically it's the HTTP internals like `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse` where we do our monkey patching. So far as Im aware at least!

The goal being to collect them in one place, decide how to deal with them, push anything we can to node core or otherwise eliminate them. 

This is a stub issue rn, hoping folks can collaborate and report places where we do this so we can track and discuss them. I have an actual write up about these issues, some history, and specifics that I'll dig up and probably edit into this or otherwise link to.

I am aware of specifically `on-headerss` and the `res.writeHead` we realized during https://github.com/jshttp/on-headers/security/advisories/GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q

What else? 

Our practice of extending the proto of `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse` to create our `(req, res)` also falls into this category

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @bjohansebas 2025-08-09T00:27:56Z:
**Monkey patching**

* **In compression:** We do monkey patching on `ServerResponse` methods: `.write`, `.end`, `.on`, `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In express-session:** We do monkey patching on `ServerResponse` methods: `.end`, `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In connect-timeout:** We do monkey patching on `ServerResponse` methods: `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In response-time:** Monkey patching on `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In cookie-session:** Monkey patching on `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In morgan:** Monkey patching on `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In on-headers:** :( — `.writeHead`.
* **In express:** We alter the prototype of `ServerResponse` and `IncomingResponse`. We could follow a style similar to Fastify: store the original response in a property called `.raw`, and define methods that call those properties, which would then be passed to the router. This would also help enable HTTP/2, so that middleware doesn’t need to overwrite things to use HTTP/2. Instead, through the compatibility layer and ALPN negotiation, middleware could work normally — similar to how Fastify does it (Probably I didn’t explain very well how to do it, but I hope to share the idea in more detail soon)

Those are the modules I noticed; feel free to comment on where else we do monkey patching.

comments.body:
We want to track down and document all instances of express and our core deps monkey-patching Node core, specifically it's the HTTP internals like `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse` where we do our monkey patching. So far as Im aware at least!

The goal being to collect them in one place, decide how to deal with them, push anything we can to node core or otherwise eliminate them. 

This is a stub issue rn, hoping folks can collaborate and report places where we do this so we can track and discuss them. I have an actual write up about these issues, some history, and specifics that I'll dig up and probably edit into this or otherwise link to.

I am aware of specifically `on-headerss` and the `res.writeHead` we realized during https://github.com/jshttp/on-headers/security/advisories/GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q

What else? 

Our practice of extending the proto of `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse` to create our `(req, res)` also falls into this category

comments.author: bjohansebas
comments.body:
**Monkey patching**

* **In compression:** We do monkey patching on `ServerResponse` methods: `.write`, `.end`, `.on`, `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In express-session:** We do monkey patching on `ServerResponse` methods: `.end`, `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In connect-timeout:** We do monkey patching on `ServerResponse` methods: `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In response-time:** Monkey patching on `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In cookie-session:** Monkey patching on `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In morgan:** Monkey patching on `.writeHead` (on-headers).
* **In on-headers:** :( — `.writeHead`.
* **In express:** We alter the prototype of `ServerResponse` and `IncomingResponse`. We could follow a style similar to Fastify: store the original response in a property called `.raw`, and define methods that call those properties, which would then be passed to the router. This would also help enable HTTP/2, so that middleware doesn’t need to overwrite things to use HTTP/2. Instead, through the compatibility layer and ALPN negotiation, middleware could work normally — similar to how Fastify does it (Probably I didn’t explain very well how to do it, but I hope to share the idea in more detail soon)

Those are the modules I noticed; feel free to comment on where else we do monkey patching.

thread_text:
ISSUE #6614: location function does not validate potentially malicious URLs
Author: xzyingxiashubro
Date: 2025-06-30T15:36:35Z
Labels: bug
State: closed

[c0]
## Bug: location function does not validate potentially malicious URLs

## Environment information

**Version**: express 5.0.0-beta.3

**Platform**: Linux

**Node.js version**: 18.x

**Any other relevant information**: N/A

## What steps will reproduce the bug?

1. Create an Express application
2. Set up a route that uses `res.location()` with a malicious URL
3. Send a request to this route and observe the response headers

```js
const express = require('express');
const app = express();

app.get('/redirect', (req, res) => {
  // Set a malicious URL in the Location header
  res.location('javascript:alert("XSS attack")');
  res.status(302).send('Redirecting...');
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log('Server running on port 3000');
});

// Using curl to test:
// $ curl -i http://localhost:3000/redirect
//
// The response headers will contain:
// Location: javascript:alert("XSS attack")

```

## What is the expected behavior?
The location function should validate the URL scheme and reject or sanitize non-HTTP(S) URLs, especially those with potentially dangerous schemes like javascript:, data.

## What happens instead?
The function sets the malicious URL directly in the Location header without any validation:
```
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: javascript:alert("XSS attack")
...
```
This creates a security vulnerability as browsers following this redirect might execute the JavaScript code, leading to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks.

## Source of the issue
The issue is in the location function in lib/response.js.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @SantiagoCecena 2025-07-03T20:23:20Z:
Hi,

I'm interested in working on this issue.

The current behavior of `res.location()` allowing `javascript:` or `data:` schemes in the `Location` header poses a significant **XSS vulnerability**, as browsers might execute such malicious URLs. While `encodeUrl` handles URL encoding, it doesn't validate the safety of the URL scheme itself.

I'd like to propose adding a **scheme validation** step within the `res.location` function. This would involve checking if the provided URL starts with safe schemes like `http://`, `https://`, or is a relative path (`/`). Any other schemes (e.g., `javascript:`, `data:`) would be rejected or handled safely to prevent this type of attack.

I believe this enhancement would significantly improve the **default security of Express** for all users.

Would it be possible for me to pick this up and submit a pull request? I'm happy to discuss the implementation details further.

Thanks,
Santiago
---
[c2] @ctcpip 2025-07-03T21:36:53Z:
Hi, please note our [threat model](https://github.com/expressjs/security-wg/blob/main/docs/ThreatModel.md#the-express-threat-model) is clear that it is the application's responsibility to control what is passed to methods, including `res.location()`.  Furthermore, there are perfectly valid use cases for non http schemes in location headers.
---

title: res.redirect cannot carry the request header I set
need_summary: The developer needed to know if custom headers (e.g., an id header) can be preserved or altered during an HTTP redirect, and the answer cites RFC 9110 §15.4 (and the Firefox source list) indicating redirects cannot add or remove custom headers except for security‑sensitive ones like Authorization or Cookie.
security_topic: custom request headers are not preserved across HTTP redirects
question_text: res.redirect cannot carry the request header I set
answer_text:
2. and 3. as far as I know are impossible. Redirections are described in RFC 9110 in section [15.4. _Redirection 3xx_](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#status.3xx). The RFC says (emphasis mine):
> When automatically following a redirected request, **the user agent SHOULD resend the original request message** with the following modifications:
>
> 1. Replace the target URI with the URI referenced by the redirection response's [Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.location) header field value after resolving it relative to the original request's target URI.
> 2. Remove header fields that were automatically generated by the implementation, replacing them with updated values as appropriate to the new request. This includes:
>    1. (...)
> 3. Consider removing header fields that were not automatically generated by the implementation (i.e., those present in the request because they were added by the calling context) where there are security implications; this includes but is not limited to [Authorization](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.authorization) and Cookie.
> 4. Change the request method according to the redirecting status code's semantics, if applicable.
> 5. If the request method has been changed to GET or HEAD, remove content-specific header fields, including (but not limited to) [Content-Encoding](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-encoding), [Content-Language](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-language), [Content-Location](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-location), [Content-Type](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-type), [Content-Length](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.content-length), Digest, [Last-Modified](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#field.last-modified).

In general, the user agent (e.g. browser) sends the original request, but changes some necessary automatically generated headers (e.g. `Host`) and **removes headers that may have security implications such as `Authorization` and `Cookie`**. The list of removed headers will probably depend on the user agent - [here is the list from Firefox](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/6cc05c6620814bf3eb05278ccf3b1f49690b7740/netwerk/protocol/http/HttpBaseChannel.cpp#123-148).
The RFC does not offer a way of adding or removing custom headers when redirecting a request - whatever was in the original request is in the redirected one (with the exceptions mentioned above).

title: Express 5.1: req.body is `undefined` when using express.json() for requests that do not have a request body
need_summary: The change to have req.body be undefined instead of {} in Express 5 is intentional and documented in the Express migration guide (see https://expressjs.com/en/guide/migrating-5.html#req.body).
security_topic: change in req.body initialization behavior
question_text: Why is req.body undefined in Express 5.1 when using express.json() for requests that do not have a request body?
answer_text: This was actually an intentional change in v5 and is documented in the migration guide (https://expressjs.com/en/guide/migrating-5.html#req.body). This enables an app to disambiguate an empty body and a non‑existent body.
thread_text:
ISSUE #6432: Express 5.1: req.body is `undefined` when using express.json() for requests that do not have a request body
Author: booherbg
Date: 2025-04-03T18:01:56Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
Simply put, with express 5.1 req.body is `undefined` when not explicitly including a request body. This is unexpected! In express 4.x, req.body is guaranteed to be at least `{}` even when the request body is missing.

# Express 5.1 Bug Report: express.json() Middleware Body Initialization

## Environment information

**Version**:
```json
"dependencies": {
  "express": "5.1.0"  // Broken behavior
  "express": "4.21.2" // Working behavior
}
```

**Platform**:
```bash

$ uname -a
 24.2.0 Darwin Kernel Version 24.2.0: Fri Dec  6 18:40:14 PST 2024; root:xnu11215.61.5~2/RELEASE_ARM64_T8103 arm64
```

**Node.js version**:
```bash
$ node -v
v22.9.0
```

## What steps will reproduce the bug?

1. Create minimal Express server:
```javascript
const express = require('express');
const app = express();

app.use(express.json());

app.post('/test', (req, res) => {
  console.log('Body:', req.body);
  res.json({ receivedBody: req.body });
});

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Server running on port 3000'));
```

2. Send POST request with no body:
```bash
$ npm install express@5
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/test
Server Output: `Body: undefined`
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/test -H "Content-Type: application/json"
Server Output: `Body: undefined`

$ npm install express@4
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/test
Server Output: `Body: {}`
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/test -H "Content-Type: application/json"
Server Output: `Body: {}`
```

3. Observe behavior:
- Express 4.x: `req.body` is `{}`
- Express 5.x: `req.body` is `undefined`

## Expected Behavior
When a POST request is made with no body (with or without `Content-Type: application/json`), the `express.json()` middleware should initialize `req.body` to an empty object `{}`, as it did in Express 4.x.

## Actual Behavior
In Express 5.x, `req.body` is `undefined` when no body is sent, even when the request includes `Content-Type: application/json`.

This change breaks backward compatibility and affects common REST API patterns where routes expect `req.body` to be an object, even if empty.

Example output:
``` bash
$ npm install express@5
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/test
# Server Output: `Body: undefined`
$ npm install express@4
# Server Output: `Body: {}`
```

--- COMMENTS ---

This was actually an intentional change in v5 and is [documented in the migration guide](https://expressjs.com/en/guide/migrating-5.html#req.body).

This enables an app to disambiguate an empty body and a non-existent body.

I'd like to point out that the [API reference](https://expressjs.com/en/5x/api.html#express.json) says

> A new body object containing the parsed data is populated on the request object after the middleware (i.e. req.body), **or an empty object ({}) if there was no body to parse, the Content-Type was not matched, or an error occurred.**

[c8] @SakarDev 2025-05-03T22:30:44Z:
There are multiple workarounds
### Solution 1
To force it behave like `Express 4.x` Change the line `app.use(express.json());` to

```
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  express.json()(req, res, (err) => {
    if (!req.body) req.body = {};
    next(err);
  });
});
```

### Or Solution 2
Add a global middleware to ensure `req.body` is never undefined
```
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  req.body = req.body || {};
  next();
});
app.use(express.json());

```

$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/test -H "Content-Type: application/json"
Server Output: `Body: undefined`

$ npm install express@4
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/test
Server Output: `Body: {}`
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/test -H "Content-Type: application/json"
Server Output: `Body: {}`
```

3. Observe behavior:
- Express 4.x: `req.body` is `{}`
- Express 5.x: `req.body` is `undefined`

## Expected Behavior
When a POST request is made with no body (with or without `Content-Type: application/json`), the `express.json()` middleware should initialize `req.body` to an empty object `{}`, as it did in Express 4.x.

## Actual Behavior
In Express 5.x, `req.body` is `undefined` when no body is sent, even when the request includes `Content-Type: application/json`.

This change breaks backward compatibility and affects common REST API patterns where routes expect `req.body` to be an object, even if empty.

Example output:
``` bash
$ npm install express@5
$ curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/test
# Server Output: `Body: undefined`
$ npm install express@4
# Server Output: `Body: {}`
```

This enables an app to disambiguate an empty body and a non-existent body.

comments.author: krzysdz
comments.body:
@Adam-Golan If you are using regular expressions directly, then yes - `\w` is a character class that matches word characters. However if you are using `'\w'` as a part of a string literal then it is equivalent to just `'w'` (try `console.log('\w')`). If you want a string to contain a backslash, then it has to be escaped (`'\\'`).

In both Express 4 and 5 you can pass a regular expression directly as a path (e.g. `app.get(/^\/files\/(\w+\.(?:jpe?|pn)g)$/i, (req, res) => { /*...*/ })`), but it has to be [`instanceof RegExp`](https://github.com/pillarjs/router/blob/e6d6b609fc355e558174ccd5b1db646f739fe88c/lib/layer.js#L50). Also in regular expressions `*` is a quantifier and quantifiers apply to immediately preceding token. There cannot be a quantifier that immediately follows another one (except for `?`, which makes the previous one lazy) like in `**`.

According to [Express Playground Router](https://bjohansebas.github.io/playground-router/) in Express 4, the route expression `'/**'` is converted to `/^\/(.*)(.*)$/i` RegExp (`*` was just converted to `(.*)`), which has two capture groups, and the second one is always empty (quantifiers are greedy by default, so `.*` in the first group matches everything after `/`). `*` in Express 4 was just an unnamed capture group that matches anything - even an empty sequence.

In Express 5, `*` behaves differently and must be followed by name - wildcards are no longer unnamed and match at least one character. A `'/*literallyAnythingAsAName'` route is converted to `/^(?:\/([\s\S]+))(?:\/$)?$/i` RegExp. Wildcard segments are [converted to `[\s\S]+`](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/blob/f4f51b70220a15c2c72afe4d4df12c7cb5844a18/src/index.ts#L584).

In summary:
- `'/**'` in Express 4 would match everything and create `req.params[0]` and `req.params[1]` (`[1]` always empty) - just use `'/*'`,
- `'/**'` in Express 5 is invalid, because wildcard parameters require a name and `*` is not a valid one - `'/*"*"'` would work and capture `req.params['*']`, that has at least one character,
- `'/*\w'` is the same as `'/*w'` (that's how string literals in JS work) and in Express 5 would create a wildcard parameter that captures at least one character in `req.params.w`.

I really recommend experimenting with @bjohansebas' [Express Playground Router](https://bjohansebas.github.io/playground-router/) if you want to understand how Express handles routes.

title: [Need] Add client hello for request
need_summary: The developer asked whether Express can provide the TLS client‑hello for JA3 fingerprinting, and the answer references the Express security best‑practice documentation (recommending TLS termination via Nginx) and the read‑tls‑client‑hello npm package.
security_topic: accessing TLS client hello data for JA3 fingerprinting in Express
question_text: I don't know if this can be supported in express.
answer_text:
[This documentation on security best practices](https://expressjs.com/en/advanced/best-practice-security.html#use-tls) states

> In general, we recommend Nginx to handle TLS

So, support for this may not be available out of the box (though, I'm not 100% certain) and that may be intentional.

For a pure JS implementation, there is the `read-tls-client-hello` package, though it's a bit outdated.

Please see our security reporting guidelines.

As for a fix for the example, that one uses `ejs` and should use the template for the `p` tag. A PR would be welcome to fix this example.

title: Unpatched `path-to-regexp` ReDoS in 0.1.x (CVE-2024-52798, CVE-2024-45296)
need_summary: The developer needed to know how to fix the ReDoS vulnerability and the TypeError caused by updating path-to-regexp, and the answer was to pin the dependency to version 0.1.12 (e.g., npm install path-to-regexp@0.1.12 --save-exact)
security_topic: regression after updating path-to-regexp to fix ReDoS vulnerability
question_text: When forcibly updating to version 0.1.12, an error occurs: TypeError: pathRegexp is not a function.
answer_text:
in v4, path-to-regexp is actually pinned: "path-to-regexp": "0.1.12"

anyway, this was patched in [4.21.2](https://github.com/expressjs/express/releases/tag/4.21.2)

Author: dbas-dn

Labels: awaiting more info

[c0]
[CVE-2024-52798](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/security/advisories/GHSA-rhx6-c78j-4q9w)
[CVE-2024-45296](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9wv6-86v2-598j)

A new vulnerability has appeared in a dependent package. 
When forcibly updating to version 0.1.12, an error occurs: TypeError: pathRegexp is not a function.


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @dbas-dn 2024-12-09T09:33:46Z:
I’ve noticed an issue with how pnpm handles automatic vulnerability fixes. When a package version is updated, pnpm uses the >= prefix, for example:
```
"path-to-regexp@<0.1.12": ">=0.1.12"
```
This allows pnpm to install any version starting from 0.1.12 and above, including newer major versions like 3.3.0. However, this can lead to compatibility issues if the package consuming the dependency is not prepared for a major version upgrade.
To avoid this problem, I suggest replacing >= with either:
* ^ to limit the updates within the same major version, or
* <1.0.0 if the dependency needs to stay within the same major version range.
For example:
```
"path-to-regexp": ">=0.1.12 <1.0.0"
```
This would ensure that the installed version stays below 1.0.0, preventing unexpected major version upgrades while still addressing vulnerabilities.
---
[c2] @dbas-dn 2024-12-09T09:36:03Z:
In any case, the version of the dependent package should be updated. There are no changes that could break the express package:
[Compare versions v0.1.10 & v0.1.12](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/compare/v0.1.10...v0.1.12)

[c7] @blakeembrey 2024-12-09T22:17:40Z:
@viceice I would recommend opening that as a new issue, but unfortunately in the process of trying to fix the CVE in V4 I had to sacrifice some previously valid paths due to ambiguity in the `path-to-regexp@0.1` paths. To solve your specific problem immediately I would recommend switching to path array feature of Express, so it would look like:

```js
['/-/verdaccio/data/package/readme/@:scope/:package/:version?', '/-/verdaccio/data/package/readme/:package/:version?']
```

This isn't ideal, but the way the backtracking protection has been written is that it assumed everything prior to the parameter was regular characters, while clearly `(` in this case is not. I think we could discard `(` and `)` (when un-escaped) without any ill side effect but other special characters will have the same issue.

title: ETag should consider CORS headers
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether the ETag should vary with the Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin header to prevent CORS security errors, and the answer cites RFC 9110 and RFC 9111 which define the handling of 304 responses and caching of CORS headers.
security_topic: ETag handling with CORS headers
question_text: I want the ETag to change when the `access-control-allow-origin` header is different but the response body is the same.
answer_text:
From my own dive into the RFCs, this is a nasty problem with how the 304 response is defined and how headers work in HTTP caches, including caches inside web browsers:

* [RFC 9110](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html): Hypertext Transfer Protocol
  * [8.8.3](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#field.etag): ETag
    * Opaque validator for different representations of _the resource_
    * Headers are not part of the resource -- if the ETag had to change when the headers changed, then the ETag would be useless in letting a cache extend the lifespan of a stale cached response because the new expiration time would force a new ETag, even though there is no theoretical reason to transmit the entire body again
  * [15.4.5](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#status.304): 304 Not Modified
    * Appropriate response for a conditional GET or HEAD when the response _would be_ a 200 (OK), except the request indicated that the client already had "a valid representation" of "the target resource", and the client must use its stored representation as if it were the content of a 200.
    * Lists headers a server `MUST` generate in a 304 and states that it `SHOULD NOT` send any others "unless said metadata exists for the purpose of guiding cache updates".
      * Must include `Content-Location`, `Date`, `ETag`, `Vary`, `Cache-Control`, and `Expires`.
      * Does not list anything related to Access-Control, including `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` or `Access-Control-Allow-Certificate`. Does not, in any way, refer to headers implicated by the `Vary` field.
* [RFC 9111](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html): HTTP Caching
  * [3.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#storing.fields): Storing Header and Trailer Fields
    * Cache all the headers, including the headers the cache doesn't understand or care about, except for a handful of specific headers about the connection itself, for proxy-to-cache negotiation, or those explicitly named in cache directive headers as "exclude from cache".
    * Nothing in particular is said about `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so it must be cached.
  * [4](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#constructing.responses.from.caches): Constructing Responses from Caches
    * Only use the cached content if the URI matches, the header fields match, the response isn't uncacheable (unless it passes validation), and the stored response is fresh, it validates, or can be served stale.
    * Always use the most recent version available.
  * [4.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#caching.negotiated.responses): Calculating Cache Keys with the Vary Header Field
    * Somewhat contradicts the story in 4 -- while 4's "unless it passes validation" is specifically applied to the "don't cache" header and "expired", 4.1 explicitly describes Vary also allowing revalidation.
    * If the cache has a mix of responses for the URI, some of which have `Vary` headers and some of which don't, it should prefer responses with a "valid" Vary field value, making the responses with no such header functionally useless in the cache.
  * [4.3.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#validation.sent): Sending a Validation Request
    * Synthesize a request by copying the method, URI, and those specific headers identified by Vary, then add preconditions to solicit 304 responses if the answer matches stuff already in the cache
  * [4.3.2](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#validation.received): Handling a Received Validation Request
    * If conditions + your data say you can serve a 304, serve a 304
  * [4.3.4](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#freshening.responses): Freshening Stored Responses upon Validation
    * "Update" means "replace the headers in the stored response" -- see [RFFC 9111 3.2](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#update), which says "add new headers, overwrite existing headers, follow the exceptions in 3.1, if you're patching together different requests or adding/removing compression then update those parts to match"
    * Update those stored responses that have matching validators

The upshot to all this:

* A strictly standards-compliant server giving a 304 response should omit the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header; thus, an intermediate cache receiving updated `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` headers during successful revalidation, and subsequently sending a 304 of its own, is expected _not_ to propagate that updated header
* A strictly standards-compliant cache receiving a 304 response should update its cached headers for every response it stored on that path with matching validators; thus, a cache at any level (including a web browser) receiving updated `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` headers should rewrite the header stapled to cached prior requests from other origins

Therefore, ACAO with values other than `*` can only successfully transit caches if every single cache along the way is strategically violating the spec:

* It has to send updated ACAO headers anyway
* It must avoid writing "updated" ACAO headers back to cache rows pertaining to `Vary: origin` requests with different origins, even when the validators match

If it doesn't do both of these things, then at some point a downstream client is going to process a response with an ACAO header that doesn't match the Origin and treat this as a security error. If the ACAO headers get dropped along the way, a request coming in from a new-but-acceptable origin will not see the new ACAO response specifying the origin from the request. If the ACAO headers get propagated, and written back to cached rows as the spec demands, then we get similarly broken results from a sequence of requests: request from origin A, miss cache, receive 200 (cache it), propagate response; request from origin B, revalidate, receive 304 (additional cache row sharing content, update headers), patch cached body onto new ACAO header; request from origin A, hit cache, respond with the cached response and headers -- _which now includes the ACAO header from origin B_ because the cache _must_ use the most recent headers.

It's not hard to imagine a way to do this "right": always send the ACAO header and don't cross-update headers for other cache rows pertaining to the same request path when those requests varied in some relevant dimension (according to the `Vary` header). This violates the spec but works as intended. If _every cache along the way_ chooses to violate the spec in this way, ACAO works as intended.

Patching a hash of the `ACAO` header onto the end of the Etag -- or similar -- avoids header cross-contamination by, morally, treating the ACAO header as part of the content, thereby forcing unchanged content to re-transfer as an undesirable side effect of HTTP caching semantics, where caches are encouraged to strip relevant headers and required to cross-update headers based on _resource_ validators that specifically do not cover the header.

Removing the ETag does not help. Per [RFC 9111 4.3.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#validation.sent), the cache is allowed to use timestamps instead, even when a `Vary` header should make everyone involved kind of sus that timetsamps don't tell enough of the story. As far as the spec is concerned, if the server wanted to be clear that the timestamp isn't enough to identify a content revision, it should use Etag...

Patching a CDN to emit ACAO headers on a 304 response _does_ help but if there are more caches along the way (caching proxies, end-user browser caches), _those_ caches are free to exhibit the same behaviors.
thread_text: ISSUE #5986: ETag should consider CORS headers Author: IchordeDionysos Date: 2024-09-25T16:22:17Z Labels: State: open [c0] TL;DR: I want the ETag to change when the `access-control-allow-origin` header is different but the response body is the same. --- We are facing an issue right now with a couple moving parts working poorly together. It's a bit difficult to explain but I'll try my best. 1. When sending a request from Chrome to a spec-compliant CDN, it will initially hit the express server. 1. The express server responds with the resource, CORS & Vary headers, and an ETag derived from the response body. 2. The CDN will cache the response headers and body. 3. Chrome will also cache the response headers and body. 2. When Chrome requests the resource from a different origin, it may take the ETag cached for a different Origin and send it to the CDN (this is spec-compliant). 1. This may then lead the CDN to respond with a 304 Not Modified, as the CDN may have a resource for the origin and ETag in the cache. 2. Responding with 304 will only return partial headers (explicitly excluding CORS headers; Some spec says it should NOT return CORS headers here). 3. This then leads Chrome to take the response from the cache and think that the Origins mismatch → throwing a CORS error. This is kind of messed up, as all parties do comply with the specs, though when put together, the specs don't work nicely together. comments.author: IchordeDionysos
comments.body: TL;DR: I want the ETag to change when the `access-control-allow-origin` header is different but the response body is the same. --- We are facing an issue right now with a couple moving parts working poorly together. It's a bit difficult to explain but I'll try my best. 1. When sending a request from Chrome to a spec-compliant CDN, it will initially hit the express server. 1. The express server responds with the resource, CORS & Vary headers, and an ETag derived from the response body. 2. The CDN will cache the response headers and body. 3. Chrome will also cache the response headers and body. 2. When Chrome requests the resource from a different origin, it may take the ETag cached for a different Origin and send it to the CDN (this is spec-compliant). 1. This may then lead the CDN to respond with a 304 Not Modified, as the CDN may have a resource for the origin and ETag in the cache. 2. Responding with 304 will only return partial headers (explicitly excluding CORS headers; Some spec says it should NOT return CORS headers here). 3. This then leads Chrome to take the response from the cache and think that the Origins mismatch → throwing a CORS error. This is kind of messed up, as all parties do comply with the specs, though when put together, the specs don't work nicely together. The best way to fix this would be for the server to generate a different ETag when the `access-control-allow-origin` header differs.

comments.author: AdamNorberg
comments.body:
From my own dive into the RFCs, this is a nasty problem with how the 304 response is defined and how headers work in HTTP caches, including caches inside web browsers:

* [RFC 9110](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html): Hypertext Transfer Protocol
  * [8.8.3](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#field.etag): ETag
    * Opaque validator for different representations of _the resource_
    * Headers are not part of the resource -- if the ETag had to change when the headers changed, then the ETag would be useless in letting a cache extend the lifespan of a stale cached response because the new expiration time would force a new ETag, even though there is no theoretical reason to transmit the entire body again
  * [15.4.5](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#status.304): 304 Not Modified
    * Appropriate response for a conditional GET or HEAD when the response _would be_ a 200 (OK), except the request indicated that the client already had "a valid representation" of "the target resource", and the client must use its stored representation as if it were the content of a 200.
    * Lists headers a server `MUST` generate in a 304 and states that it `SHOULD NOT` send any others "unless said metadata exists for the purpose of guiding cache updates".
      * Must include `Content-Location`, `Date`, `ETag`, `Vary`, `Cache-Control`, and `Expires`.
      * Does not list anything related to Access-Control, including `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` or `Access-Control-Allow-Certificate`. Does not, in any way, refer to headers implicated by the `Vary` field.'
* [RFC 9111](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html): HTTP Caching
  * [3.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#storing.fields): Storing Header and Trailer Fields
    * Cache all the headers, including the headers the cache doesn't understand or care about, except for a handful of specific headers about the connection itself, for proxy-to-cache negotiation, or those explicitly named in cache directive headers as "exclude from cache".
    * Nothing in particular is said about `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so it must be cached.
  * [4](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#constructing.responses.from.caches): Constructing Responses from Caches
    * Only use the cached content if the URI matches, the header fields match, the response isn't uncacheable (unless it passes validation), and the stored response is fresh, it validates, or can be served stale.
    * Always use the most recent version available.-
  * [4.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#caching.negotiated.responses): Calculating Cache Keys with the Vary Header Field
    * Somewhat contradicts the story in 4 -- while 4's "unless it passes validation" is specifically applied to the "don't cache" header and "expired", 4.1 explicitly describes Vary also allowing revalidation.
    * If the cache has a mix of responses for the URI, some of which have `Vary` headers and some of which don't, it should prefer responses with a "valid" Vary field value, making the responses with no such header functionally useless in the cache.
  * [4.3.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#validation.sent): Sending a Validation Request
    * Synthesize a request by copying the method, URI, and those specific headers identified by Vary, then add preconditions to solicit 304 responses if the answer matches stuff already in the cache
  * [4.3.2](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#validation.received): Handling a Received Validation Request
    * If conditions + your data say you can serve a 304, serve a 304
  * [4.3.4](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#freshening.responses): Freshening Stored Responses upon Validation
    * "Update" means "replace the headers in the stored response" -- see [RFFC 9111 3.2](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#update), which says "add new headers, overwrite existing headers, follow the exceptions in 3.1, if you're patching together different requests or adding/removing compression then update those parts to match"
    * Update those stored responses that have matching validators

The upshot to all this:

* A strictly standards-compliant server giving a 304 response should omit the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header; thus, an intermediate cache receiving updated `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` headers during successful revalidation, and subsequently sending a 304 of its own, is expected _not_ to propagate that updated header
* A strictly standards-compliant cache receiving a 304 response should update its cached headers for every response it stored on that path with matching validators; thus, a cache at any level (including a web browser) receiving updated `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` headers should rewrite the header stapled to cached prior requests from other origins

Therefore, ACAO with values other than `*` can only successfully transit caches if every single cache along the way is strategically violating the spec:

* It has to send updated ACAO headers anyway
* It must avoid writing "updated" ACAO headers back to cache rows pertaining to `Vary: origin` requests with different origins, even when the validators match

If it doesn't do both of these things, then at some point a downstream client is going to process a response with an ACAO header that doesn't match the Origin and treat this as a security error. If the ACAO headers get dropped along the way, a request coming in from a new-but-acceptable origin will not see the new ACAO response specifying the origin from the request. If the ACAO headers get propagated, and written back to cached rows as the spec demands, then we get similarly broken results from a sequence of requests: request from origin A, miss cache, receive 200 (cache it), propagate response; request from origin B, revalidate, receive 304 (additional cache row sharing content, update headers), patch cached body onto new ACAO header; request from origin A, hit cache, respond with the cached response and headers -- _which now includes the ACAO header from origin B_ because the cache _must_ use the most recent headers.

It's not hard to imagine a way to do this "right": always send the ACAO header and don't cross-update headers for other cache rows pertaining to the same request path when those requests varied in some relevant dimension (according to the `Vary` header). This violates the spec but works as intended. If _every cache along the way_ chooses to violate the spec in this way, ACAO works as intended.

Patching a hash of the `ACAO` header onto the end of the Etag -- or similar -- avoids header cross-contamination by, morally, treating the ACAO header as part of the content, thereby forcing unchanged content to re-transfer as an undesirable side effect of HTTP caching semantics, where caches are encouraged to strip relevant headers and required to cross-update headers based on _resource_ validators that specifically do not cover the header.

Removing the ETag does not help. Per [RFC 9111 4.3.1](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#validation.sent), the cache is allowed to use timestamps instead, even when a `Vary` header should make everyone involved kind of sus that timetsamps don't tell enough of the story. As far as the spec is concerned, if the server wanted to be clear that the timestamp isn't enough to identify a content revision, it should use Etag...

Patching a CDN to emit ACAO headers on a 304 response _does_ help but if there are more caches along the way (caching proxies, end-user browser caches), _those_ caches are free to exhibit the same behaviors.

comments.author: azadsingh99
comments.body:
The problem arises because the ETag, which is a unique identifier for a resource, is generated based only on the resource's content, not considering the origin making the request. When a browser like Chrome requests a resource from one origin, it caches the response, including the ETag. Later, if Chrome requests the same resource from a different origin, it may reuse the cached ETag and send it to the CDN.

The CDN checks its cache and might return a "304 Not Modified" response, meaning the resource hasn't changed. 304 Not Modified responses don’t include CORS headers. Without the CORS headers, Chrome assumes the origins don’t match and throws a CORS error.

To fix this, the server should include the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header value when generating the ETag. This makes the ETag unique for each origin, ensuring the CDN caches and serves resources correctly for different origins. It prevents Chrome from reusing the wrong ETag and avoids the CORS error entirely.

comments.author: jonchurch
comments.body:
I've spent the day with this scenario and learned quite a lot.

For anyone who hasn't read the full context, this is not an Express bug. It may be an edgecase of your application, depending on someone's infrastructure/CDN configuration, but is not specific to your HTTP framework of choice

Interpretting specs can be confusing, so if you think I have made a mistake in my response plz do correct me and link me to the right info.

My understanding per the Fetch spec is that a browser initiated conditional request will not replace headers of the cached reponse upon receipt of a 304, but will merge the headers. That's outlined in the [http-network-or-cache-fetch](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#http-network-or-cache-fetch) algorithm (step 10 substep 4, wish I could link), which links out to [RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching): Freshening Responses](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9111.html#freshening.responses).

In this browser-managed revalidation case, the 304 response itself is not exposed to JavaScript. Instead, Fetch produces a final response using the previously cached response (after header updates), and the CORS check is applied to that final response, not to the bare 304. A 304 therefore does not bypass or suppress CORS; it simply participates in cache validation.

As a result, a CORS error would only occur if the final revalidated response fails the CORS check for the requesting origin. In modern browsers, HTTP cache partitioning typically prevents cross-origin reuse of cached responses, making this class of issue rare.

This type of 304 CORS issue was documented pre 2020 before browsers started partitioning their cache by origin. [Here is Tim Berners Lee complaining about it in 2017 ](https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/www-archive/2017Aug/0000.html). Browers partitioning cache by origin essentially solved CORS errors on 304 by accident.

If someone wants to dig deeper on the issue, you'll need to be able to reproduce it. For all the discussion in this thread of specs and edgecases, it would help quite a lot if someone could stand up a reproduction and share their source and CDN configuration. That would go a long way towards providing guidance for someone who finds themselves with these errors in their application. I don't like the idea of tweaking ETAGs, but providing someone the flexibility to do so given a good reason is feasible. I think what express can offer folks is documentation of this issue, if it is shown to be relatively easy to get yourself into today, and suggestions for fixing it.

title: Dependency: Bump path-to-regexp in v4 to fix security vulnerability.
need_summary: The developer needed to know which version of path-to-regexp fixes the GHSA-9wv6-86v2-598j vulnerability, and the answer cites version 0.1.10 (and later) with the advisory URL as the concrete reference.
security_topic: identifying scanner source and fixing vulnerable path-to-regexp version
question_text: Is the scanner Snyk? Because we have asked them [to change theirs here](https://github.com/expressjs/express/pull/5902#issuecomment-2344000830)
answer_text:
Snyk has already updated [their advisory](https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-PATHTOREGEXP-7925106), listing 0.1.10 as not vulnerable.

**How to fix?**

Upgrade `path-to-regexp` to version 0.1.10, 1.9.0, 3.3.0, 6.3.0, 8.0.0 or higher.

With the added note recommending 8.0.0 if possible and warning of custom regular expressions:

**Note:** While the 8.0.0 release has completely eliminated the vulnerable functionality, prior versions that have received the patch to mitigate backtracking may still be vulnerable if custom regular expressions are used. So it is strongly recommended for regular expression input to be controlled to avoid malicious performance degradation in those versions. This behavior is enforced as of version 7.1.0 via the strict option, which returns an error if a dangerous regular expression is detected.

title: Crash after starting using version 4.21.0
need_summary: The crash is due to a regression in path‑to‑regexp where non‑string paths aren’t coerced, and applying the patch that changes `path = path.replace` to `path = String(path).replace` (see commit 29b96b4a1de52824e1ca0f49a701183cc4ed476f) resolves it.
security_topic: regression in express 4.21.0 caused by non-string route handling in path-to-regexp
question_text:
I just updated express to fix the latest reported CVEs, but the last version (4.21.0) is now causing crashes when loading express.

Crash happens when I call this:
`const express = require("express")`

Error is:
```
...\node_modules\path-to-regexp\index.js:68
  path = path.replace(
              ^

TypeError: path.replace is not a function
    at pathToRegexp (...\node_modules\path-to-regexp\index.js:68:15)
    at new Layer (...\node_modules\express\lib\router\layer.js:45:17)
    at Function.route (...\node_modules\express\lib\router\index.js:505:15)
    at app.<computed> [as put] (...\node_modules\express\lib\application.js:498:30)
    at Object.<anonymous> (...\js\index.js:69:9)
    at Module._compile (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1254:14)
    at Module._extensions..js (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1308:10)
    at Module.load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1117:32)
    at Module._load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:958:12)
    at Function.executeUserEntryPoint [as runMain] (node:internal/modules/run_main:81:12)
``` 

I realize this is not the express library, but express is the only user of `path-to-regexp` in my application, so it can't be any other culprit.

The exact same code on my side runs fine using for example express 4.19.2.
answer_text:
From looking over the various places that resulted in this bug, I believe this was never intended to work and the documentation is wrong. As a result, I'm working through these steps and you should remove these lines of code from your application since they didn't do anything before:

1. Introduce a clearer error in `path-to-regexp`
2. Remove this documentation from expressjs.com (which is under `app.use`, I believe it was a mistaken clarification)

If you want this code that previously did not run, to run, you can set the route to `*` as mentioned here: https://github.com/expressjs/express/issues/5955#issuecomment-2346874034

The route was getting garbled to symbols of function. For example, I can’t think of any native object that could coerce and still match a real route. title: Express 5.0.0 Route with regex not working
need_summary: The developer needed to know that Express 5 removed regex support in route strings for security (ReDoS) reasons and should use an array of paths or a custom regex, as documented in the Express 5 migration guide (https://expressjs.com/en/guide/migrating-5.html#path-syntax).
security_topic: removal of regex route support due to ReDoS risk
question_text: Is it realtes to https://blakeembrey.com/posts/2024-09-web-redos/ and https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9wv6-86v2-598j? But I don't understand, why the major version of "path-to-regexp" was updated when express@5 was released?
answer_text:
We will be recommending folks use a more robust input validation approach for this. If you want, here is the open api library I maintain: https://github.com/wesleytodd/express-openapi/

The reason for this is mainly security around DOS protection. There is no way to support path segment regular expression matching while also avoiding major performance regressions. See more here: https://blakeembrey.com/posts/2024-09-web-redos/

This is a 100% big win for the ecosystem longer term, as regular expression route matching was one of the worst decisions from the early days which has stuck around. So while we understand the pain this change will cause, we stand by this decision as the right thing for the ecosystem and all express users (even if you need to change your approach to this sort of routing).

Author: HarishGangula
Date: 2024-09-11T07:08:51Z
Labels: 5.x
State: closed

[c0]
We have created simple express application with following code 

```

const express = require('express')
const app = express()
const port = 4000

function logErrors(err, req, res, next) {
    console.error(err.stack)
    next(err)
}

function clientErrorHandler(err, req, res, next) {
    if (req.xhr) {
        res.status(500).send({ error: 'Something failed!' })
    } else {
        next(err)
    }
}
function errorHandler (err, req, res, next) {
   
    res.status(err.statusCode || 500)
    res.json({ message: err.message || "something wrong" })
}

app.get('/', async (req, res) => {
    await Promise.reject({"message":"dsfjh", statusCode: 400})
    res.status(200).send("asfas")
})

app.get('/[discussion|page]/:slug', async (req, res) => {
    throw {statusCode: 400, message: "harish"}
    res.status(200).send("asfas")
})


app.use(logErrors)
app.use(clientErrorHandler)
app.use(errorHandler)

app.listen(port, () => {
    console.log(`Example app listening on port ${port}`)
})

```

It is throwing following error 

```

~/express5/node_modules/path-to-regexp/dist/index.js:136
        throw new TypeError(`Unexpected ${nextType} at ${index}, expected ${type}: ${DEBUG_URL}`);
        ^

TypeError: Unexpected [ at 1, expected END: https://git.new/pathToRegexpError
    at Iter.consume (~/express5/node_modules/path-to-regexp/dist/index.js:136:15)
    at consume (~/express5/node_modules/path-to-regexp/dist/index.js:193:16)
    at parse (~/express5/node_modules/path-to-regexp/dist/index.js:197:20)
    at ~/express5/node_modules/path-to-regexp/dist/index.js:308:74
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at pathToRegexp (~/express5/node_modules/path-to-regexp/dist/index.js:308:25)
    at Object.match (~/express5/node_modules/path-to-regexp/dist/index.js:278:30)
    at matcher (~/express5/node_modules/router/lib/layer.js:83:23)
    at new Layer (~/express5/node_modules/router/lib/layer.js:90:62)
    at Function.route (~/express5/node_modules/router/index.js:421:17)
```
We identified that path to regexp node module is broken which is causing this issue.

**Node.js v20.10.0** used

But I don't understand, why the major version of "path-to-regexp" was updated when express@5 was released?
---
[c3] @wesleytodd 2024-09-11T16:39:55Z:
We fully dropped support for regular expressions in strings for routes. You can check out the docs for `path-to-regexp@8` in that repo. We will be putting together a migration guide for folks, but in this case you need to either use an array of paths or write your own regular expression (very discouraged). 

So it would become this:

```javascript
app.get(['/discussion/:slug', '/page/:slug'], async (req, res) => {
    throw {statusCode: 400, message: "harish"}
    res.status(200).send("asfas")
})
```
---
[c4] @ex1st 2024-09-11T16:57:48Z:
@wesleytodd, sad to hear, we used regexp for data type routing.

```javascript
app.get('/product/:page([0-9]+)', async (req, res) => {
```
---
[c5] @wesleytodd 2024-09-11T17:49:43Z:
We will be recommending folks use a more robust input validation approach for this. If you want, here is the open api library I maintain: https://github.com/wesleytodd/express-openapi/

The reason for this is mainly security around DOS protection. There is no way to support path segment regular expression matching while also avoiding major performance regressions. See more here: https://blakeembrey.com/posts/2024-09-web-redos/

This is a 100% big win for the ecosystem longer term, as regular expression route matching was one of the worst decisions from the early days which has stuck around. So while we understand the pain this change will cause, we stand by this decision as the right thing for the ecosystem and all express users (even if you need to change your approach to this sort of routing).
---
[c6] @blakeembrey 2024-09-11T18:53:44Z:
@HarishGangula I do want to include as an aside here that `'/[discussion|page]/:slug'` did not do what you expected in express 4 either, since `[]` is a regex character group, so this was matching `/d/x` for example. 

Due to time constraints I haven't had the capacity to write a version that supports parsing of regex characters into something that can be guaranteed safe to avoid ReDoS, but that's not a forever situation. They've been reserved so it's possible to add it back again later.

@ex1st Totally understand the concern, it's my biggest let down too. For now you'd have to include it in the method and call `next()` when it doesn't match a number. This is both good and bad, since it'll motivate people to use better validation libaries for more complex regex cases instead of trying to cram it into the path itself, but obviously for something like yours it looks like a regression.

title: npm audit fail on last Express version (4.20.0) due to send(0.19.0) vulnerability
need_summary: The developer needed a mitigation for the send <0.19.0 template‑injection vulnerability affecting Express 4.20.0, and the answer supplied a concrete overrides snippet pinning send to ^0.19.0 (referencing the GHSA‑m6fv‑jmcg‑4jfg advisory and related issue comment).
security_topic: transitive dependency vulnerability causing npm audit failure
question_text: npm audit fail on last Express version (4.20.0) due to send(0.19.0) vulnerability
answer_text:
My advice for now, if using express v4, until the maintainers actually fix this. See: Mismatched dependency versions (https://github.com/expressjs/express/issues/5943#issuecomment-2343038272)

```
  "overrides": {
    "encodeurl": "~2.0.0",
    "qs": "^6.13.0",
    "send": "^0.19.0"
  },
```

Be aware it may not be possible for every occasion if other dependencies use a completely different version. My two cents.

title: Mismatched dependency versions
need_summary: The developer asked if the vulnerable encodeurl/send/finalhandler versions used by serve‑static could be addressed, and the maintainers responded with concrete PRs (serve-static#180, finalhandler#62, express#5954) and an overrides workaround to upgrade those dependencies.
security_topic: rationale for dependency pinning in Express
question_text: Is there a reason that Express pins dependencies like this? I could _maybe_ see the argument to pin third-party packages (though I'd say this is far more uncommon than not in the JS ecosystem), but it's not clear to me why dependencies from the `expressjs`/`pillarjs` orgs are pinned since presumably those are all controlled by the same group of people and thus trusted to follow semver and not suddenly become malicious.
answer_text:
We are removing these pins in v5. This is historical from when the ecosystem was MUCH more volatile and the entire project was primarily maintained by one person. It made more sense then, it makes less sense now.

EDIT: You can see we use `^` for any that we updated [here](https://github.com/expressjs/express/blob/master/package.json#L30-L63)
